title: I Can’t Do That But I Can Do This
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post addresses how leaders can decline requests without damaging relationships. It argues that every yes to someone else is a no to the leader's own priorities, so leaders must say no more often, and that the difficulty comes from wanting to be liked. The proposed move is to pair the refusal with a substitute offer: I can't do that, but I can do this. The post supplies a list of concrete example phrasings. It claims the alternative matters more as a signal of thoughtfulness than as something the requester accepts, and that people feel supported even when they decline it.
points: Saying yes to others quietly spends the leader's own priorities, which is why more refusals are required to accomplish personal goals and vision.
Offering a smaller or different form of help lets the leader keep control of their time while softening the refusal.
The substitute does not need to be accepted; the thoughtfulness of offering it is what makes the requester feel valued.
Concrete scripts, such as sending interview questions instead of conducting the interview, make the technique easy to adopt.
The approach is a polite way of telling people they matter, just not more than the work the leader must do.
quotes: Saying “No” to requests and invitations can be excruciatingly hard. Leaders don’t want to let others down or miss an important opportunity.
Unfortunately, saying “Yes” comes with a significant downside. When leaders say “Yes” to others, they are often saying “No” to their own priorities.

To soften the negative feelings leaders believe they create when saying “No,” one highly effective strategy is to replace a “Yes” with something different. In conversation, this strategy sounds like this: “I can’t do that, but I can do this.

This strategy softens the “No” by offering an alternative that allows the leader to maintain control over their time. It is not important whether this replacement is accepted as much as that it is offered.

People appreciate that a leader has been thoughtful in their reply and values their request highly enough to suggest a substitute choice. In most cases, those making the request will feel supported by the response, even if they politely decline the replacement.

The next time you must reject a request or invitation, consider the “I can’t do that, but I can do this” approach. Your willingness to help or support the request in a limited way makes your rejection more palatable. In essence, it is the polite way of telling others that they matter but not more than the work you need to do.
